title: Judge awards damages to both sides in lawsuit after neighbours' dispute over loose dogs 'spun out of control'
summary: A judge has awarded an eastern Manitoba couple sued by their neighbour $10,000 in damages, and their neighbour $1,000, after an "unfortunate series of events" unfolded over dogs allowed to run loose…

image.caption: A woman's decision to let her rescue dogs roam free on her property led to an 'unfortunate series of events' with her neighbours, a Manitoba judge wrote in a recent decision. (Reshetnikov_art/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Manitoba

A judge has awarded an eastern Manitoba couple sued by their neighbour $10,000 in damages, and their neighbour $1,000, after an "unfortunate series of events" unfolded over dogs allowed to run loose on an unfenced property.
'Robert Frost knew fences make good neighbours,' Justice Sheldon Lanchbery wrote in decision

The couple — a man and woman, named as the defendants in a lawsuit filed with Manitoba Court of King's Bench — purchased their "dream property" along the Winnipeg River, in the rural municipality of Alexander, in 2015, Justice Sheldon Lanchbery wrote in a Nov. 16 decision.
The property has a large forested area, with walking trails, that shielded them from their neighbours, and offered an escape from the "hustle and bustle of the real world," Lanchbery wrote.
Around 2017, a woman — the plaintiff in the suit — purchased the adjacent property to the east, and decided it would be "a great location" to raise rescue dogs, the decision says.

Though she lacked prior experience in handling rescues, she registered a business as a dog rescue — an idea that "originated during a course of employment on an Indigenous reserve," where dogs roamed freely, Lanchbery wrote.
She decided to also let the dogs she rescued roam on her new property.
"The dogs in question are best described as feral," Lanchbery wrote, and their "aggressive tendencies" continued post-rescue.
Justice Sheldon Lanchbery decided against awarding legal costs to either party, saying in his decision they 'were painfully aware this was not their finest hour.' (Jaison Empson/CBC)
Although the municipality had bylaws in place to restrict the number of dogs a landowner can have on their property, the woman "far exceeded that number," the judge wrote.
"The evidence as to the precise number is inconsistent," but she had at least seven prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, Lanchbery wrote.
The couple said they "did not dare go walking" in the forested area of their property because of the dogs.
The man in the couple testified one of the woman's dogs bit his shin. He also suffered a contusion on one of his hands after he punched the animal, Lanchbery wrote.
'A lot of talking, but not a lot of listening'

The woman had a dog kennel on her property, but the dogs were not always kept there and were not leashed when outside it, the decision says. The woman believed the dogs "should be able to roam," which included defecating on the couple's property.
There were early attempts to resolve the conflict, which Lanchbery described as "a lot of talking, but not a lot of listening."
Accusations "flew back and forth," and "a first-year law student knows what follows next," wrote Lanchbery.
Building a fence between their properties could have solved their problem.Justice Sheldon Lanchbery
Security cameras were installed, and both parties started to photograph and film each other near the property line.
Land surveys were also ordered and boulders were placed near where the dog owner believed the property line was, but another survey done by the couple showed she was incorrect, the decision says.
The woman then approached the couple to ask if they would help pay for a fence to keep her dogs from entering their property.
The couple refused, in part because they felt it was the woman's responsibility to control her dogs, Lanchbery wrote.
He quoted American poet Robert Frost, who "knew fences make good neighbours."
"Building a fence between their properties could have solved their problem," wrote Lanchbery.
Both sides guilty of trespassing
Disputes continued between the parties. The woman purchased a "large, cumbersome" dock, and instead of putting it on her own property, she placed it on the couple's.

"I find if the dock was to be placed in the Winnipeg River, the easiest unimpeded point of access to transport the dock into the Winnipeg River was on the east side of … [the dog owner's] property, not on the west side [closer to the neighbours]," wrote Lanchbery.
The couple put up "no trespassing" signs, " adding to … [the dog owner's] frustration," he wrote.
The woman later accused the couple of trespassing and filed her lawsuit, after the man threw broken boards from the dock into her dog kennel.
One of her dogs suffered an eye injury, but the judge said evidence suggested it likely wasn't from the boards.
The man admitted he had thrown the boards into the kennel, but denied the dog was present when he did so. There was no evidence the dog was in the kennel at the time, Lanchbery wrote.
The judge concluded, however, that both parties were guilty of trespassing — the couple by throwing the deck boards into the kennel, and the woman by letting her dogs run loose.

items: Dispute between neighbours in small Manitoba community ends with 'regrettable' court fight: judge

blocks.text: He awarded the couple $10,000 in aggravated and general damages for the woman's failure to control her dogs, which was ongoing behaviour, compared to the couple's single instance of trespassing, he said.
He also awarded the couple an extra $100 because the woman placed her dock on their property, and parked cars there too, which he said was "an inconvenience at best."

Lanchbery awarded the dog owner $1,000, saying the man's conduct in throwing the boards was "especially egregious" given that he has previous military experience, including training other members in hand-to-hand combat.
The couple's lawyer had argued that given that background, the man had actually "exercised great restraint in not injuring" the woman's dogs, but the judge rejected that argument.
"Removing boards from [her] dock and propelling them into a run are an intentional act of intimidation," he wrote.
The judge decided awarding legal costs to either party was not justified, given their conduct throughout the dispute.
"When the testimony concluded in this action, the litigants were painfully aware this was not their finest hour," he wrote.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ozten Shebahkeget is a member of Northwest Angle 33 First Nation, born and raised in Winnipeg. She started writing for CBC Manitoba during the first Pathways program in 2022. She holds a master's degree in writing from the University of Saskatchewan.
